questions.stem:
A 20-month-old girl has had fever to 39.4 C (102.9 F) for 5 days. She has injected bulbar conjunctivae that spare the area around the cornea, with no discharge; red, cracked, bleeding lips; a bright red tongue; a blanching rash over her trunk; and swollen hands with red palms sharply demarcated at the wrists. She is fussy but alert, and her blood pressure is normal for age.

Test: Result: Reference range
Leukocytes: 18,900/mm3, 76% neutrophils: 5,500 to 15,500/mm3
Platelets: 490,000/mm3: 150,000 to 400,000/mm3
Albumin: 2.7 g/dL: 3.5 to 5.0 g/dL
Urine: White cells, no organisms, culture pending: No white cells

Which test should be obtained now, at presentation?
choices: Lumbar puncture with spinal fluid culture
Echocardiogram to assess the coronary arteries
Skin biopsy of the rash with immunohistochemistry
Rapid antigen test for influenza from the nose
Serum IgM antibody against parvovirus B19
questions.note:
**Once Kawasaki disease is diagnosed, an echocardiogram at presentation is needed because untreated disease can cause coronary aneurysms.**

Fever for 5 days with nonexudative conjunctivitis that spares the limbus, cracked red lips and a red tongue, a polymorphous rash, and swelling and redness of the hands and feet meets the criteria for Kawasaki disease. Supporting labs are a neutrophil-predominant leukocytosis, a high platelet count, low albumin, and sterile pyuria.

Kawasaki disease is a medium vessel vasculitis, and up to 20% of untreated children develop coronary artery abnormalities including aneurysms. An echocardiogram at presentation sets a baseline for the coronaries and looks for myocarditis, and treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin and aspirin follows.

Lumbar puncture with spinal fluid culture: incorrect. A lumbar puncture is not part of the standard workup for this picture, and nothing suggests meningitis.

Echocardiogram to assess the coronary arteries: correct. An echocardiogram at presentation provides a baseline for the coronary arteries and checks for myocarditis in Kawasaki disease.

Skin biopsy of the rash with immunohistochemistry: incorrect. Immunohistochemistry of a skin biopsy is one way to diagnose Rocky Mountain spotted fever, which has a petechial rash after tick exposure.

Rapid antigen test for influenza from the nose: incorrect. Influenza testing does not address this child's mucocutaneous findings or the cardiac risk.

Serum IgM antibody against parvovirus B19: incorrect. Parvovirus B19 causes a slapped-cheek rash, not this combination of conjunctival, oral, and extremity changes.

questions.stem:
A 16-year-old girl on her menstrual period has had 2 days of fever, profuse vomiting and diarrhea, and muscle aches, and today she nearly fainted on standing. Blood pressure is 60/40 mm Hg supine, pulse 160/min, and capillary refill 6 seconds. She has total body erythroderma most intense on the inner thighs, palms, and soles, injected conjunctivae, and enlarged tongue papillae. Platelets are 70,000/mm3 (150,000 to 400,000) and bicarbonate 12 mEq/L (22 to 28). Her mother, who uses the same tampon brand, has never had a similar illness.

Which of the following best explains why adolescents and young adults are at higher risk than older adults for this illness?
choices: They have fewer T cells that can respond to superantigens
They are more often colonized by toxin-producing streptococci
They have not yet developed late complement components
They lack neutralizing antibody against the toxin
They have more P antigen expressed on their red cells
questions.note:
**Toxic shock syndrome is more likely in younger people who lack neutralizing antibody to the staphylococcal or streptococcal toxin.**

Fever, shock, diffuse erythroderma including the palms and soles, mucosal hyperemia, and multiorgan involvement (low platelets, acidosis) in a menstruating adolescent is staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome, driven by the superantigen toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 from Staphylococcus aureus.

Toxic shock is more likely in younger people who have no neutralizing antibody to the toxin made by the infecting Staphylococcus aureus or group A streptococcus. Older adults have usually been exposed to the toxin before and carry antibody that neutralizes it, which is why the staphylococcal form peaks at ages 15 to 35.

They have fewer T cells that can respond to superantigens: incorrect. Young people do not have fewer responsive T cells; the problem is that nothing neutralizes the toxin before it reaches them.

They are more often colonized by toxin-producing streptococci: incorrect. The menstrual, tampon-associated form is caused by Staphylococcus aureus, not streptococci.

They have not yet developed late complement components: incorrect. Late complement components are present from infancy, and their deficiency predisposes to Neisseria, not toxic shock.

They lack neutralizing antibody against the toxin: correct. Toxic shock is more likely in people with no neutralizing antibody to the toxin, as is common in adolescents.

They have more P antigen expressed on their red cells: incorrect. The P antigen is the parvovirus B19 receptor and plays no role in toxic shock.

questions.stem:
A 10-month-old girl had 3 days of high fever, irritability, and decreased appetite with no cough, runny nose, or diarrhea. On the third day, the fever broke suddenly and a pink, discrete, blanching, nonitchy rash appeared on her trunk, spreading to the face, neck, and limbs over 2 days. She is fully immunized. She is now afebrile, well appearing, eating and drinking, and has palpable occipital nodes. Her buccal mucosa is normal.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
choices: Reassurance and supportive care
Serum measles IgM and airborne isolation
Blood culture and intravenous ceftriaxone
Echocardiogram and intravenous immunoglobulin
Throat culture and oral penicillin
questions.note:
**Roseola is diagnosed clinically from high fever followed by rash after the fever breaks in a well infant, and it needs only supportive care.**

An infant with several days of high fever whose rash appears only after the fever subsides, who is well appearing with occipital nodes and a normal buccal mucosa, has roseola (exanthem subitum) from human herpesvirus 6. HHV-6 accounts for a large share of emergency visits for febrile infants 6 to 12 months old, and infection approaches 100% by age 2.

Roseola is a clinical diagnosis in an otherwise healthy child, and it resolves on its own, so reassurance and supportive care are appropriate. The timing of rash after defervescence is the key feature: in measles and the other viral exanthems, rash appears while the child is still febrile.

Reassurance and supportive care: correct. Roseola is a clinical diagnosis in a well infant, and it resolves with supportive care.

Serum measles IgM and airborne isolation: incorrect. Measles is unlikely in an immunized infant with no cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, or Koplik spots, and its rash comes during fever.

Blood culture and intravenous ceftriaxone: incorrect. A well-appearing afebrile infant with a blanching rash does not need empiric treatment for meningococcal sepsis.

Echocardiogram and intravenous immunoglobulin: incorrect. Kawasaki disease needs at least 5 days of fever and mucocutaneous findings this infant does not have.

Throat culture and oral penicillin: incorrect. Scarlet fever is a disease of school-aged children with pharyngitis and a sandpaper rash.

questions.stem:
An 11-month-old unvaccinated boy has had 5 days of fever to 40.4 C (104.8 F). On day 3 he developed a harsh cough and was treated with amoxicillin for presumed pneumonia without improvement. Today a morbilliform rash began on his head and spread to his trunk and limbs. He has red conjunctivae and is irritable. He attends a home daycare with three other infants, and his mother asks for how long he may have been spreading the illness.

This child was most contagious during which of the following periods?
choices: Only while the rash is visible on the trunk
From about 4 days before to 4 days after the rash
Only after the rash fades and the skin peels
For up to 6 weeks, through virus in the stool
Only during the 10 days before the cough began
questions.note:
**Measles is most contagious from about 4 days before to 4 days after the rash, so spread starts during the prodrome.**

High fever with cough and conjunctivitis followed by a morbilliform rash that starts on the head and spreads downward in an unvaccinated infant is measles. Measles is one of the most contagious infections: about 9 of 10 susceptible contacts develop disease, spread is airborne and by direct contact, and the incubation period is about 10 to 12 days.

Patients are most contagious from about 4 days before to 4 days after the rash appears, so this child was spreading virus during the prodrome, before anyone suspected measles. That is why unvaccinated contacts in the daycare are at risk.

Only while the rash is visible on the trunk: incorrect. Spread begins days before the rash, during the cough and fever, not only while the rash is visible.

From about 4 days before to 4 days after the rash: correct. Measles is most contagious from about 4 days before to 4 days after the rash appears.

Only after the rash fades and the skin peels: incorrect. Contagiousness falls after the rash, so the recovery phase is not the main risk period.

For up to 6 weeks, through virus in the stool: incorrect. Prolonged shedding in stool describes the live oral polio vaccine virus, not measles.

Only during the 10 days before the cough began: incorrect. The incubation period after exposure is not the contagious window; spread peaks around the rash.

questions.stem:
A 16-year-old boy who moved to the US from Central America 8 months ago, with no vaccine records, has 3 days of fever to 39.9 C (103.8 F), myalgia, headache, and nausea. Red bumps appeared on the back of his neck and upper back on day 2. Today he has more than 500 lesions over his body, some papules, some fluid-filled vesicles, and some open and crusting, plus lesions on his conjunctiva and in his mouth. He appears ill.

Which drug is most appropriate for this patient?
choices: Penicillin
Doxycycline
Acyclovir
Azithromycin
Clindamycin
questions.note:
**Varicella (lesions in different stages) is treated with acyclovir or valacyclovir in patients ill enough to need therapy.**

Fever followed by a vesicular rash that begins centrally and contains papules, vesicles, and crusted lesions at the same time is varicella, primary infection with varicella zoster virus, a DNA herpesvirus. Lesions in different stages separate it from smallpox and mpox, where all lesions are in the same stage. An unvaccinated adolescent with hundreds of lesions and mucosal involvement is ill enough to treat.

Varicella zoster infections are treated with the antiviral acyclovir (or valacyclovir). Antibacterial drugs do not act on the virus.

Penicillin: incorrect. Penicillin treats group A streptococcal infection, such as scarlet fever, and has no activity against varicella zoster virus.

Doxycycline: incorrect. Doxycycline treats rickettsial infection such as Rocky Mountain spotted fever, not a herpesvirus.

Acyclovir: correct. Acyclovir is the antiviral used for varicella zoster virus infection.

Azithromycin: incorrect. Azithromycin is used for pertussis, not viral infections.

Clindamycin: incorrect. Clindamycin is added for toxin-mediated staphylococcal and streptococcal disease, not for varicella.

questions.stem:
A 15-year-old boy is admitted overnight with fever, chills, severe muscle pain, and a rash that went from macular to petechial to purpuric within hours. Spinal fluid shows a gram-negative diplococcus. The next morning his best friend, a teammate on his basketball team, comes to clinic. They shared water bottles at practice 2 days ago and rode home in the same car. The friend feels well and has a normal examination.

Which of the following is the most appropriate management for the friend?
choices: No action unless he develops a fever
Intravenous immunoglobulin as a single dose
Oral ciprofloxacin as soon as possible
Oral azithromycin for 5 days
A pneumococcal conjugate vaccine dose
questions.note:
**Close contacts exposed to the oral secretions of a meningococcal case receive chemoprophylaxis (rifampin, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone), ideally within 24 hours.**

A petechial and purpuric rash with a gram-negative diplococcus in spinal fluid is invasive meningococcal disease from Neisseria meningitidis, which colonizes the nasopharynx and spreads through respiratory and throat secretions. The friend shared water bottles, so he was directly exposed to the patient's oral secretions in the 7 days before symptoms.

Chemoprophylaxis is the main way to prevent secondary cases of sporadic meningococcal disease. It is given to household members, child care contacts, and anyone exposed to the patient's oral secretions, ideally within 24 hours of identifying the index case, using rifampin, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone.

No action unless he develops a fever: incorrect. Waiting for fever is too late, because invasive disease can progress to shock within hours.

Intravenous immunoglobulin as a single dose: incorrect. Immunoglobulin is used in Kawasaki disease and streptococcal toxic shock, not for meningococcal exposure.

Oral ciprofloxacin as soon as possible: correct. A contact exposed to oral secretions should receive chemoprophylaxis such as ciprofloxacin as soon as possible.

Oral azithromycin for 5 days: incorrect. Azithromycin is the prophylaxis for pertussis contacts, not for meningococcus.

A pneumococcal conjugate vaccine dose: incorrect. A pneumococcal vaccine does not protect against Neisseria meningitidis.

questions.stem:
A 5-year-old boy had a sore throat, then 2 days of fever, vomiting, and severe left knee pain with a limp. In the emergency department his temperature is 40.0 C (104 F), pulse 183/min, and blood pressure 87/57 mm Hg. The knee is aspirated and the fluid is cloudy. A red rash spreads from his lower leg over his entire body, and he develops kidney and liver injury. Blood and joint fluid cultures grow beta-hemolytic gram-positive cocci in chains. He is taken for washout of the knee.

Clindamycin is added to his beta-lactam antibiotic mainly to accomplish which of the following?
choices: Cover methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus in the joint
Neutralize toxin that is already circulating in the blood
Improve penetration of the antibiotic into spinal fluid
Prevent rheumatic fever after the throat infection
Stop the bacteria from making new superantigen toxin
questions.note:
**In toxic shock syndrome, a protein synthesis inhibitor such as clindamycin is added to stop toxin production, and IVIG neutralizes toxin in the group A strep form.**

Shock, a spreading erythematous rash, and multiorgan failure with beta-hemolytic streptococci in the blood and a septic joint after a sore throat is streptococcal toxic shock syndrome from group A streptococcus. Its exotoxins act as superantigens, driving T cell proliferation and an overwhelming release of interleukin 1, interleukin 2, interferon gamma, and tumor necrosis factor alpha that causes shock.

Treatment of toxic shock uses anti-streptococcal or anti-staphylococcal antibiotics usually including one that inhibits protein synthesis, such as clindamycin, because it shuts down production of the toxin itself. Toxin that is already circulating is addressed by intravenous immunoglobulin, which is added for the group A streptococcal form.

Cover methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus in the joint: incorrect. The culture shows streptococci in chains, not staphylococci, so resistant Staphylococcus aureus coverage is not the reason.

Neutralize toxin that is already circulating in the blood: incorrect. Neutralizing circulating toxin is the role of intravenous immunoglobulin, not clindamycin.

Improve penetration of the antibiotic into spinal fluid: incorrect. Nothing here suggests meningitis, and spinal fluid penetration is not why clindamycin is added.

Prevent rheumatic fever after the throat infection: incorrect. Rheumatic fever prevention is not the purpose; the goal is to stop toxin production during shock.

Stop the bacteria from making new superantigen toxin: correct. A protein synthesis inhibitor such as clindamycin stops the bacteria from making more superantigen toxin.
